subtype: Approach: measuring use before changing it [Thinking]

Tuesday
Aparna Didi dared me to open the screen-time page. I said fine, it'll be about two hours.
Six hours and eleven minutes. Daily average. Four and a half of that on short videos.
I actually felt my face go hot. Six hours is a whole school day. Where did it go? Mostly between 10 pm and 1 am, the report says, and in tiny bits: two minutes, three minutes, forty times.
My usual move would be to feel terrible, delete everything tonight and reinstall on Thursday. Done that twice already. This time I'm going to use the numbers instead. The biggest block is late night, so that's where I start. The short-video app is the main thing, so that gets a limit first, not messages with friends.
Target for this week: under five hours, and nothing after 11.
Checking again Sunday. Numbers, not guilt.
– Nilesh

subtype: Approach: asking what need the phone is meeting [Thinking]
passage:
Zainab, you asked on the student podcast how I cut down my night scrolling. I'm Dolma, and here's the honest answer: I stopped asking how to stop, and asked why I was doing it.
One night I wrote down what I felt right before I picked up the phone. Three nights running, it was the same two things. First, lonely. We'd moved to Delhi in June and I didn't really have anyone yet. Second, homework dread. The maths I hadn't started sat on the desk like a rock, and scrolling meant I didn't have to look at it.
So the phone was doing two jobs, badly. I gave those jobs to better things. For lonely: I call my old friend in Gangtok at nine, ten minutes, voice only. For dread: I open the maths and set a ten-minute timer. Just ten. Usually I keep going.
I still scroll sometimes. Just not till two.

qa.q: When does Dolma call the old friend in Gangtok?
qa.a: At nine, for ten minutes, voice only.

qa.q: What two feelings did Dolma find before picking up the phone?
qa.a: Dolma felt lonely after the move to Delhi, and full of dread about the maths homework.

qa.q: What else could Dolma do about the loneliness in Delhi?
qa.a: Join one club or activity at the new school, so there are people nearby to talk to as well as the old friend.

qa.q: How might the old friend in Gangtok feel about the nine o'clock calls?
qa.a: The friend probably enjoys staying close and feels valued, perhaps without knowing the calls replaced scrolling.

grounding: Shows a student asking what the night scrolling is for, finding loneliness and homework dread, and planning a friend call and ten-minute homework starts instead.

subtype: Approach: asking what need the phone is meeting [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Deepak, and Pallavi and I share a room, so I see her phone light up the ceiling most nights. Until last month it glowed till one.
Then one evening she sat on the bed with a notebook and asked me something odd: “When do you think I pick it up?” I said, “When you're bored?” She shook her head and wrote for a while. Later I saw the page. Two words circled: “alone” and “tests”.
She said it out loud, more to herself than to me: “I scroll when I miss my Mumbai friends, and when I'm scared to start chemistry.”
Now, around nine, she calls someone called Hina and laughs for ten minutes. Then she sets a kitchen timer for ten minutes and starts chemistry. The timer rings; usually she ignores it and keeps going.
The ceiling's been dark by eleven most nights. I don't know if she's less lonely. She seems lighter, though.

qa.q: What two words were circled on Pallavi's page?
qa.a: Alone and tests.

qa.q: What does Pallavi saying "I scroll when I miss my Mumbai friends" reveal?
qa.a: It shows she felt lonely and scared about chemistry, and had worked out that the phone was covering those feelings.

qa.q: What else could Pallavi try if the call and the timer stop working?
qa.a: Talk to a teacher or the school counsellor about settling in, so the loneliness gets real support beyond one call a night.

qa.a: Deepak notices the ceiling dark by eleven and Pallavi seeming lighter, though Deepak can't be sure how she feels inside.

subtype: Approach: if-then rules and phone-free zones [Action]
passage:
Kishore wrote his two rules on the inside of his study-table drawer in their Chandigarh flat, where no one else would see them.
If I sit down to study, the phone goes to the shoe rack by the door.
If it's after ten, the phone sleeps on the hall charger.
The first evening he forgot rule one and found himself twenty minutes into a video with his physics book open. He got up, walked the phone to the shoe rack and came back. The second evening he did it without much thought. By the second week he didn't have to decide at all; sitting down meant the phone went.
His friend Baljeet noticed on Saturday. “You've been replying late.”
“It's on the hall charger after ten,” Kishore said. “Rule.”
“Your rule or your parents'?”
“Mine. That's why it works.”
His test marks that month rose only a little. But he was asleep before eleven most nights.

qa.q: Where does Kishore's phone go when he sits down to study?
qa.a: To the shoe rack by the door.

qa.q: How does Kishore seem to feel about the rules by the second week?
qa.a: He seems relieved and confident, since the rules had become automatic and no longer needed a decision.

qa.q: What else could Kishore add if the phone still pulls at the study table?
qa.a: Keep a clock or timer on the desk, so there is no reason to fetch the phone to check the time.

qa.q: How do the rules look to Baljeet?
qa.a: Baljeet first notices only the late replies, then learns the rules are Kishore's own, which may make them seem worth copying.

grounding: Shows a teen using if-then rules, phone out of the room during study and on the hall charger after ten, until the choice becomes automatic.

subtype: Approach: app limits and removing triggers [Action]
passage:
Hrithik, you keep asking how I get so much done without looking at my phone. I wasn't born like this. When I was in Class Eleven, my mother used to say, “Jahnavi, that phone owns you.” She was right.
One Sunday I made a list and did everything on it in one sitting. First, I deleted the two short-video apps. Not logged out; deleted. Second, I set a one-hour daily limit on messaging, so after that the app went grey. Third, I turned off every notification except calls and my mother's messages. Fourth, the hardest: I moved my games off the phone onto the old family computer in the drawing room. If I wanted to play, I had to walk there, switch it on and wait. Usually I decided I didn't want to that much.
Did I become perfect? No. But my phone got boring, and boring was exactly what I needed. So, Hrithik, start with the notifications. That one's easiest.

qa.a: Onto the old family computer in the drawing room.

qa.a: Jahnavi seemed relieved, even pleased, because a boring phone was exactly what was needed.

qa.q: Which step in the story made games a deliberate choice, and why did it work?
qa.a: Moving them to the family computer, because walking there and waiting gave time to decide it wasn't worth it.

qa.a: The mother, who used to say the phone owned Jahnavi, would likely have been relieved and surprised to see it set aside.

subtype: Approach: app limits and removing triggers [Action]

Preeti couldn't just put the phone away. Her coaching classes ran on it, with the timetable, the recorded lectures and the test links, and the family had no laptop. So on Saturday she tried something else, with her brother Saurabh reading out the settings.
She deleted the short-video app and the one with endless reels. She put a forty-five-minute daily limit on messaging, enough for the class groups. She switched off every notification except calls, coaching and her parents. The two games she loved went onto Saurabh's old tablet, which lived in the steel cupboard; playing meant asking for the key.
On Monday she opened the phone for a lecture, and nothing else lit up. On Wednesday the messaging app went grey at 8 pm. She sighed and went back to her notes.
By Friday she had asked for the cupboard key only once.

qa.a: A forty-five-minute daily limit.

Rehana, your father was just like you at fifteen, only his screen was the video-game box plugged into our television. Every evening, four, five hours. We tried hiding the cable. He sulked on the sofa, bored stiff, and found the cable within two days. Taking the game away didn't work, because nothing took its place.
Then your grandfather did something clever. The colony boys played cricket on the maidan every evening, and he walked your father there and said, “You bowl, beta, you have the height.” And on Sundays I sent him to Master Joseph's guitar class, because he was always drumming on the dining table anyway.
Within a month he was coming home at seven, sweaty and starving, and falling asleep over dinner. The game box gathered dust. Nobody had to hide anything.
So when you tell me there's nothing to do but your phone, I, your Minakshi Dadi, say: let's find your cricket.

On the first of the month, Bhupen stood up in the hostel common room and announced it: “No screens for thirty days. No phone, no laptop, nothing.” Parveen, his roommate, clapped slowly. Bhupen handed his phone to the warden to keep.
Day two: fine. Day three: he missed the message that the chemistry practical had moved to the morning, because the class group runs on messaging. He turned up late and lost marks.
Day four: the project group needed his part of the slides by night. He went to the warden, took back the phone and did the slides. Then, since the rule was broken anyway, he watched videos till one.
“So that's the thirty days,” he told Parveen the next morning, flat. “I failed. Might as well not bother.”
“You failed one version,” Parveen said. “The version where school doesn't use phones.”
But by the weekend Bhupen was back to his old hours.

qa.a: He felt defeated and flat, treating one broken day as proof the whole effort was pointless.

subtype: Approach: cold-turkey resolution announced on the first day [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Nilesh,
Remember the big announcement at Diwali? “A whole month, no screens, starting Monday”? You said I'd last a week. I lasted three days.
Here's what went wrong. I hadn't thought about the fact that everything at school happens on the class group: homework changes, test dates, the Saturday cancellation. On Thursday I missed the message that the maths test had moved, and walked in unprepared. That evening I switched the phone back on to check what else I'd missed, and then I was on it till midnight.
And then I just gave up on the whole thing. One slip, and my brain said, “Well, that's ruined, back to normal.” Normal is five hours a day.
I don't think the problem was willpower. The plan was all or nothing, and life isn't.
Want to try something smaller together? Maybe just no phone after ten?
Jatin

qa.q: What did Jatin miss on Thursday?
qa.a: The message that the maths test had moved.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel after the slip on Thursday?
qa.a: Jatin felt defeated, as if the whole plan was ruined, and gave up completely.

qa.q: What would you change first in Jatin's plan?
qa.a: Keep the class group on and cut only the time-wasting parts, like the smaller no-phone-after-ten rule Jatin now suggests.

qa.q: How might Nilesh react to this letter?
qa.a: Nilesh may tease a little about the prediction, but likely feels touched to be asked to try the smaller plan together.

grounding: Shows a student swearing off screens for a month, ignoring that school runs on messaging, breaking by day four, and giving up through all-or-nothing thinking.

Baljeet, you want to know how my big phone plan is going? I'm Deepak, king of Mondays, so let me tell you.
In July I said I'd start after the unit tests, because why start during tests. After tests there was Raksha Bandhan and cousins visiting, so obviously after that. Then it was “first Monday of September”, a clean start. That Monday I had a cold. The next Monday there was a cricket match on at night, so not a fair week. Then Navratri. Then “after Diwali, properly”.
It's almost December. I've written the plan four times, in four notebooks. It's a good plan! Phone out of the room at night, a limit on videos. I just haven't done a single day of it.
And my screen time is the same as in July. Exactly the same.
So honestly, Baljeet, what if tonight is the Monday?

subtype: Approach: promising to start on Monday [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Ritu. I sit next to Pooja, and I've been hearing about her phone plan since June.
In June it was, “After the first unit test.” In July, “After my birthday, I'm not starting in my birthday week.” In August she showed me a timetable drawn with coloured pens: phone locked in a drawer from eight to ten, one hour of videos only. “From Monday.” That Monday there was a class trip, so, “Next Monday.”
September had the Ganesh festival. October had exams, “and you can't change habits during exams, everyone knows that.”
It's November. The timetable is still in her notebook; I saw it yesterday, a bit faded. Every morning she tells me what time she slept. Last night it was two.
I don't think she's lazy. I think she's waiting to feel ready. I don't know if that feeling ever comes.

qa.a: Last night it was two.

subtype: Approach: agreeing family rules together rather than imposed ones [Action]
passage:
Two years ago our house had a phone fight at every single dinner. Papa would say, “Put that away, Uma,” while his own phone buzzed beside his plate. Mummy, whose name is Shalini and who hates being told what to do, took my side more than once.
So one Sunday we had what Papa called a family meeting and I called a negotiation. I said I'd accept rules if I helped make them and if they applied to everyone. We agreed on two: no phones at meals, for all four of us, and every device on the kitchen shelf by ten, including Papa's work phone unless he's on call.
The first week Papa broke it twice, and my little brother fined him five rupees each time. That's when it stopped feeling like a punishment for me and started feeling like our house's thing.
We still mostly keep it. Dinners got longer.

qa.q: What two rules did the family agree on?
qa.a: No phones at meals for all four of them, and every device on the kitchen shelf by ten.

qa.a: Uma felt the rules were fair, less like a punishment and more like something the whole house owned, which was a relief.

qa.q: What else could keep the rules working over time?
qa.a: A quick family check every few months to adjust them, so they stay agreed together rather than slowly becoming imposed.

qa.a: Papa may find them inconvenient at first, but paying the fines shows he accepts being held to the same standard.

grounding: Shows a teen and parents agreeing together on no devices at meals and after ten, with the parents keeping the same rule, so it feels shared rather than a punishment.

subtype: Approach: agreeing family rules together rather than imposed ones [Action]

Counsellor's note, family meeting, Thursday
Afreen's parents came to me last week worried about her phone use at night, and I suggested that instead of rules from above, the family agree them together. Today Afreen came with both parents and her grandmother, Lakshmi, and I mostly listened.
Afreen's first reaction, arms folded, was, “So it's a punishment.” Her mother surprised her: “No. We'll follow it too. I'm on my phone at dinner more than you.” That changed the room.
They agreed on three things: no devices at meals, all phones in a basket by the door at ten, and whoever breaks it washes the dishes the next day. Lakshmi, who has no phone, volunteered to be the judge.
By the end Afreen was negotiating details, weekends till eleven, instead of resisting. They left laughing about who would lose first. I will check in with Afreen in two weeks.

qa.a: They wash the dishes the next day.

qa.q: What does Afreen's folded-arms reaction suggest at first?
qa.a: It suggests she felt defensive and resentful, expecting the rules to be a punishment aimed only at her.

qa.q: What else could the family agree on to make the rules last?
qa.a: A short review after a month, where everyone, Afreen included, can suggest changes like the weekend time.

qa.q: How might Afreen's mother feel admitting her own phone use at dinner?
qa.a: She may feel a little exposed, but relieved to turn it into a shared family effort rather than a fight.

subtype: Approach: seeking help when control keeps failing [Revision]

Darshan, you think asking for help means you've failed. Let me tell you about me at sixteen.
I tried everything with my phone. I made timetables. I deleted apps and reinstalled them. I gave the phone to my mother at night, then took it back. Three plans in one term, and I was still gaming till three, falling asleep in chemistry, and my marks slid from the seventies to the fifties.
One night I sat at the kitchen table and said to Appa and Amma, “I can't fix this alone.” Amma said, “Joseph, then we don't do it alone.” The next day the three of us went to the school counsellor. She didn't scold. She helped us build a fixed routine: school, football, homework, phone in the hall at nine. And she said if that wasn't enough, she'd help us find further support outside school.
It took months. But it started with saying it out loud.

With Appa on night shifts at the textile mill and Amma leaving at six for the hospital canteen, nobody was awake to see Karthik's phone glowing at two. He'd tried three plans since June: app limits he kept switching off, a timetable, and giving the phone to his younger brother Chinmay, who handed it back whenever asked nicely.
His half-yearly marks came home in November, down in almost every subject. He'd fallen asleep in two tests.
That Sunday, the one morning both parents were home, Karthik put the report card on the table. “I've tried. It isn't working. I need help.”
Amma read it twice. On Monday she swapped shifts and went with him and Appa to the school counsellor. The counsellor mapped out a fixed routine, with the phone in Chinmay's room overnight and study hours at school, and said that if things didn't improve, she'd help them find a professional outside school.
Karthik was asleep by eleven that night, for once.

qa.q: What else might help Karthik with no parent awake at night?

qa.a: Chinmay may feel trusted but a little burdened, now holding the phone for real rather than handing it back when asked.
